abort.devices_mode_not_offered: Devices mode is not available in this preview. This build sets the integration up for diagnostics only -- it polls the inverter and can run the capability diagnosis, but creates no sensors. Promotion will be offered in a later release, and the entry does not need to be removed and added again when it is.
abort.wrong_device: That address answers as a different inverter ({model}), not the one behind “{title}”. Nothing was changed. Each inverter keeps its own entry; to add that one, use Add integration.
abort.connection_unchanged: That is the connection this entry already uses. Nothing was changed.
abort.connection_moved: “{title}” now uses the new connection. It has been reloaded; its entities, their history and its settings are unchanged.

error.no_serial_number: The device answered but reported no serial number.
error.unrecognized_inverter: The device answered with an unknown model code ({code}). Please open an issue with this code so the model can be added.
error.legacy_package_still_loaded: The YAML package is still running, so its entities still hold their IDs. Remove `modbus_sungrow.yaml` from your configuration — or comment out the line that includes it — then restart Home Assistant and try again. Or choose Start fresh.
error.network_too_large: That range holds {hosts} addresses, more than the limit of {limit}. Sweeping it would take minutes and flood the network. Narrow it to the subnet the inverter is on, usually a /24.

entity_ids.title: Existing entities found
entity_ids.description:
Home Assistant found **{count} entities** from the `modbus_sungrow.yaml` package, such as `{example}`. Your recorder history, your statistics and every dashboard card are stored against those entity IDs.

{status}

**Migrate my existing entities** takes those IDs over. History and statistics carry on uninterrupted and your dashboards keep working unchanged. Nothing is copied and nothing is deleted.

**Start fresh** gives this inverter its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_pv_input_power`. Your old history stays where it is, under the old IDs, and your dashboards keep pointing at it.

Either way the entities are identical in every other respect.

data_description.entity_ids: This can be changed later without losing anything.

slot_unknown.title: Existing entities found
slot_unknown.description:
This house ran the YAML package for more than one inverter, and Home Assistant cannot tell which of them this one was. The package's serial sensors are what say so, and neither the running package nor the recorded history has this inverter's serial.

So the YAML package's entity IDs are not offered: taking the wrong set would give this inverter another inverter's history. **Submit** sets it up with its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_pv_input_power`.

To keep its old IDs, put the YAML package back for one restart, so this inverter's serial is recorded, then remove it and restart again. **Configure** can then switch this inverter to its old IDs; the serial stays on record for the recorder's retention, ten days unless you changed it.

find.title: Where is the inverter?
find.description: Searching is usually easier: many people cannot say what their inverter's IP address is without going to look at the router. The search only probes addresses on the range you confirm.

manual.title: The inverter's address
manual.description:
The inverter's IP address, and the Modbus TCP port and device address it answers on. The defaults are right for almost every installation: port 502, device address 1.

If the inverter is behind a WiNet-S dongle, this is the dongle's address rather than the inverter's own. Give the address a reservation in your router first. If it moves anyway, **Reconfigure** on the entry points it at the new one.{error}

data_description.port: 502 unless somebody changed it. A Sungrow Logger uses 503.
data_description.unit_id: 1 for a single inverter. A second inverter in a master/slave cluster answers on 2, and its own address is the one to give here.

name.title: What should this inverter be called?
name.description:
You have **{count}** inverters, and both would otherwise be called “{model}” — Home Assistant would add `_2` to whichever you set up second, which records the order you clicked in and nothing else.

This name becomes part of every entity id for this inverter, for example `{example}`. That is what your history and dashboards are keyed to, so it is worth a moment now: renaming later changes the label but leaves the ids already created exactly where they are.

Something about where it is works best — `Roof`, `Garage`, `Barn`. The suggestion is the most the inverter itself can tell us.

data_description.name: Suggested: {suggestion}. Change it to whatever you will recognise.

nothing_found.title: No inverter found

other_inverter.title: What is the other inverter?
other_inverter.description:
The make, and its size if you know it — *Fronius Symo 8.2*, or *5 kW string inverter on the south roof*. The size is the useful part: it says how large the gap in the load figures is.

This goes into the document, so leave out serial numbers, addresses and names. You can leave it blank.

pick.title: Inverters found

search.title: Search my network

testimony.title: What do you want to tell us?
testimony.description:
You chose diagnostics only, which means this entry exists to produce a reading — so these are the questions that reading needs and no register can answer.

{measured}

Everything here is optional, and leaving a field empty is honest: it records that the question was not answered, which is different from answering "I don't know". You can change any of it later under the integration's options.

Afterwards, press **Run read-only diagnosis** on the device page.

data.diagnosis_proxy: Is a Modbus proxy in the path?
data.diagnosis_other_inverter: Is there another inverter here that is not a Sungrow?
data.publish_address: May the last two octets of the address be published?
data.diagnosis_register_dump: Also sweep the raw register bands (about five minutes)

data_description.reporter: Credited in the published reading, and who gets asked if a row raises a question. Leave empty to contribute anonymously.
data_description.diagnosis_transport: Cable against dongle is measured already. What only you know is whether a dongle is on its Ethernet socket or its WiFi — a WiNet-S answers identically either way, so "not sure" is a real answer and better than a guess.
data_description.diagnosis_proxy: modbus-proxy, evcc's proxy, a Home Assistant add-on. A proxy holds one connection and lends it out, so it changes what a dropped register means — and it rebuilds every frame, which can hide or create the frame quirks this project tracks.
data_description.diagnosis_pollers: This Home Assistant is recorded automatically. What matters here is anything else: another Home Assistant, the YAML package, evcc, a logger. An inverter grants very few connections, and two clients competing for one looks exactly like a broken register.
data_description.diagnosis_other_inverter: Your Sungrow does not measure how much your house is using — it works it out from its own output plus what the grid meter says is coming in. A second inverter feeding the same meter therefore makes every load figure too low, by exactly what that inverter is producing, while everything else reads normally. No register can tell us: the Sungrow cannot see it. Say yes and we will ask what it is.
data_description.diagnosis_battery: No register reports it. "SBR096" or "Pylontech Force H1, 14.4 kWh" is more useful than a capacity the inverter already reports.
data_description.diagnosis_comment: Anything unusual about the installation — a cluster, a second inverter, a wallbox, a firmware update you remember.
data_description.publish_address: On, and yours to turn off before you submit. Only the last two octets ever reach the document — never the third, which is what would identify your network — and clear this and it reads xxx.xxx instead. What it buys is telling several readings from one house apart: a master, a slave and two dongles otherwise produce four files that look alike.
data_description.diagnosis_register_dump: On, and worth turning off if you are in a hurry. Without it a diagnosis reads the registers this integration already knows about and takes a couple of seconds. With it, it also sweeps 2181 addresses across sixteen bands, including the ones no specification documents — which is how every undocumented register this project knows was found. That is slow because an address with nothing behind it goes quiet rather than refusing, so each empty one costs a full timeout: about five minutes on a direct cable, and considerably longer through a WiNet-S or a VPN. Your inverter keeps being polled throughout, and the diagnosis button on the device page shows how far along it is.

user.title: What is this for?
user.description: {mode_intro}**The device diagnosis** connects to the inverter, works out what it is and what it answers, and creates **no entities at all**. It exists because this project has to *measure* which registers each model and firmware supports — Sungrow's own specification has been wrong in both directions — and today that evidence comes from the few houses that have sent a reading.{mode_choice}

reconfigure.title: Change the connection
reconfigure.description:
This entry reaches its inverter at **{current}**. Give the other way to reach the **same** inverter -- its own LAN port after a cable is laid, the WiNet-S dongle, or a new address.

The new connection is checked first: it has to answer with this inverter's serial number. Entity IDs, history and settings stay as they are.{error}

data_description.port: 502 unless somebody changed it. A Sungrow Logger uses 503.
data_description.unit_id: 1 for a single inverter. A second inverter in a master/slave cluster answers on 2, and its own address is the one to give here.

create_entry.default:
**You are set up.** The inverter's entities appear on its device page as their first readings arrive.

To see it in the Energy dashboard (**Settings → Dashboards → Energy**), pick the sensors [the Energy dashboard guide]({energy_dashboard_url}) names: several energy sensors have names that look right and are not.
create_entry.diagnostics:
**You are set up, and nothing has been read yet.** Two more steps, both on the device page this dialog is about to show you:

1. Press **Run read-only diagnosis**, under *Diagnostic*. It reads and never writes. On a cable it is over in a couple of minutes with the register sweep on; over a VPN it can take considerably longer, and the three sensors beside the button say how far along it is and what it is reading.
2. When it finishes, open **Notifications** in the sidebar — the badge at the bottom left. The notification there carries a summary and a **Download the document** link. That link is the JSON file to send us, and it stops working after an hour.

Missed it, or came back the next day? **Download diagnostics** on the same device page carries the same document and never expires. Send either to [the diagnosis issue]({diagnosis_issue_url}).

The file names your inverter by a stand-in rather than its serial number, and carries the last two octets of its address only while that box is ticked.

options.users: Any user who can control this device

options.direct_lan: A cable straight into the inverter's own LAN port
options.winet_lan: A WiNet-S dongle, on its Ethernet socket
options.winet: A WiNet-S dongle, but I am not sure which medium

options.yes: Yes — modbus-proxy, evcc's proxy, or a Home Assistant add-on
options.no: No, this talks straight to the inverter
options.unknown: I do not know what that is

options.yes: Yes — there is another inverter that is not a Sungrow
options.no: No — the Sungrow is the only inverter here

options.migrate: The YAML package's IDs, such as sensor.total_dc_power

options.devices_mode_coming: ⚠️ **Sensors and controls are not in this release.** This is an early alpha, and it exists to gather readings: it connects to your inverter, works out what it is and which registers it answers, and creates no entities for the values. Setting up the inverter properly -- including taking over the entity IDs of the YAML package, which decides where years of history continue -- comes in a later release, and an entry made now can be upgraded to it then without being deleted.
options.devices_mode_open: Both answers are fine, and you can change your mind later: picking **the device diagnosis** skips the weightiest question in this dialog, about which entity IDs to take over, because a reading does not need it.
options.devices_mode_intro: **Set up my inverter** is what you want if you came here to see your solar production in Home Assistant.
options.package_loaded:
⚠️ **The YAML package is still running.** {live} of its entities are live on this instance right now and are holding their entity IDs, so migrating cannot work yet.

To migrate: remove `modbus_sungrow.yaml` from your configuration — or comment out the line that includes it — then **restart Home Assistant** and add this integration again. Until then only starting fresh will work.
options.package_not_loaded: ✅ **The YAML package is not running**, so its entity IDs are free to take over. Both answers below will work.
options.switch_blocked: ⚠️ **The YAML package is still running.** {live} of its entities are live and hold the ids these would move to. Remove `modbus_sungrow.yaml` from your configuration, restart Home Assistant, and come back here.
options.wallbox_lost: **The wallbox goes quiet.** It is read through the WiNet-S today, and the inverter's own LAN port does not reach it. Its entities stay, unavailable, until **Wallbox address** in this entry's options points at the wallbox itself.
options.search_prefilled: The range below is the network Home Assistant is on, which on a home network is almost always the right one.
options.search_not_detected: **Home Assistant could not work out which network to search.** It is running in a container that can see only its own virtual network, so there is nothing here to detect your inverter's range from -- your inverter is still reachable, it just cannot be guessed at. Type the range your inverter is on, for example `192.168.1.0/24`; if you do not know it, the address of any computer on the same network gives it to you -- replace the last number with 0 and add `/24`.
options.search_same_dongle:
**Two of these are one inverter behind one WiNet-S** — its network socket and its WiFi, which have separate addresses. Modbus cannot say which is which: nothing in the protocol reports it.

It makes no difference which you pick. Both go through the same dongle to the same inverter, and both answer identically — measured on a dongle read on both of its addresses, where every register matched. If you want to know anyway, your router's client list shows them as two devices with different MAC addresses, and the WiNet-S web interface names the one it is using.
options.search_already_tried: Already searched, and nothing answered as an inverter: **{tried}**. Pick another range below, or type one. If you do not know it, the address of any computer on the same network as the inverter gives it to you -- replace the last number with 0 and add `/24`.
options.search_checked: Checked {settled} of {total} addresses; {answered} answered so far.
options.search_retry: Nothing answered. Trying again more slowly, because a busy moment can make a sweep miss a device that is there.
options.search_asking: Asking {host} what it is ({index} of {of}). Anything that is not a Sungrow has to time out on every unit id before it can be ruled out, which is the slowest part of this.
options.measured_nothing: Nothing has been measured for this address yet, so please answer from what you know.
options.measured_direct: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is **{model}**, reached through its own LAN port — register 6100 answers, which is what a cable straight into the inverter looks like.
options.measured_dongle: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is **{model}**, reached through a communication module, so a WiNet-S, WiNet-S2 or Logger is in the path — register 6100 was refused. Whether it is using its Ethernet socket or its WiFi is **not** determinable over Modbus, and that is the part only you can tell us.
options.measured_unknown: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is **{model}**, and the route could not be measured — register 6100 neither answered nor was refused, which is what a busy link looks like from here. A cable answers it and a dongle refuses it, so this is one for you to tell us.
options.load_offline: The inverter is not connected, so its load reading cannot be shown.
options.load_none: The inverter has not reported a load figure yet.
options.load_negative: Right now this inverter reports a house load of {load} W. A negative load is what an unmetered generator looks like: the house appears to be using less than nothing because something is producing that the inverter cannot see.
options.load_positive: Right now this inverter reports a house load of {load} W, which does not include anything it cannot see.
options.diagnosis_offline: The inverter is not connected, so nothing has been measured yet.
options.diagnosis_direct: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is {model}, reached through its own LAN port — register 6100 answers, which no communication module forwards.
options.diagnosis_dongle: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is {model}, reached through a communication module, so a WiNet-S, WiNet-S2 or Logger is in the path — register 6100 was refused. Whether it is using its Ethernet socket or its WiFi is not determinable over Modbus, and that is the part only you can tell us.
options.diagnosis_unknown: Already measured, so you do not need to tell us: this is {model}, and the route could not be measured — register 6100 neither answered nor was refused, which is what a busy link looks like. A cable answers it and a dongle refuses it, so this one is for you to tell us.
options.diagnosis_fitted: A communication module is fitted and names itself {module}, which is a different question from which path this endpoint is: a house can have a dongle and a cable at once.
options.battery_offline: The inverter is not connected, so nothing can be read from it.
options.battery_none: No battery is connected, so this setting does nothing.
options.battery_sungrow: {reported}, which matches a Sungrow {model}. Its datasheet gives {conservative} W conservatively ({nominal} W nominal), and that is what is used.
options.battery_bms: {reported}, which is not a Sungrow SBR or SBH. Its BMS reports a maximum charge current that works out to about {suggestion} W at the pack's current voltage — which reads high at a high state of charge, so treat it as a starting point.
options.battery_no_bms: {reported}, and its BMS does not report a maximum charge current, so there is nothing to derive one from. Without a value here the integration falls back to {fallback} W, which is the YAML package's default rather than a recommendation.
options.restore_some_refused: some registers would not take the write. Check that nothing else is polling the inverter, then try again.
options.switch_renames: **{count}** move, history and statistics with them:
options.switch_joins: **{count}** continue the YAML package's history under its ids; what was recorded under the current ids stays there:
options.switch_archives: **{count}** ids already hold older history, which is renamed aside first, not deleted:
options.switch_dropped: **{count}** raw sensors exist with legacy ids only and are removed; their history stays where it is.
options.switch_nothing: Nothing to move: every entity is already there, or has an id you chose yourself, which is left alone.

preview_release.title: Sungrow Modbus is a preview
preview_release.description:
This integration is a preview release, for testers rather than for a system you depend on.

**Entity names may still change.** A name supplies an entity id when the entity is first created, so a change does not move the ids you already have -- your history and dashboards are safe. What it does mean is that your ids can end up differing from somebody who installs later. Where that matters, a rename will ship with a migration that moves yours across and carries the history with it.

**What is not in flux:** readings, units, and the migration from the YAML package. If you chose to keep the YAML package's entity ids, those are reproduced exactly and none of this touches them.

Please report anything that looks wrong -- that is what a preview is for.

confirm.title: Put these settings back
confirm.description:
The control write test changes a setting, checks it, and changes it back. This one did not get to the changing-back part — Home Assistant was restarted, the entry was reloaded, or the inverter stopped answering partway through.

These settings may still be holding the test's values rather than yours:

{registers}

Fixing this writes each of them back and reads it again to check it took.

The following will be written back to your inverter and then read again to confirm:

{registers}

If anything refuses the write, nothing is hidden — you will be told which and this will stay here. The usual cause is something else polling the inverter at the same time.

Could not put everything back: {error}

This repair stays open so you can try again.

init.title: Sungrow Modbus options
init.description:
Everything this integration lets you change, in one place. Open a section to see it; what you do not open stays as it is.

Connection details are not here — changing the host or the unit id means talking to a different device, which is **Reconfigure** rather than an option.

data_description.add_devices: This entry was set up for diagnostics only, so it has no entities. Ticking this asks the one question that was skipped — whether to take over the YAML package's entity ids — and then creates them.{devices_mode}
data_description.entity_ids: Which IDs this inverter's entities have. Changing it moves them, with their history and statistics; the next page says exactly what moves before anything does.

polling.name: Polling
polling.description: Registers are read in four groups, each fetched as one cycle at the interval you set. {tiers} A Sungrow accepts very few Modbus connections, so if something else polls it (the YAML package, another Home Assistant, EVCC, a logger), slowing a group down or setting it to 0 (never read, its entities not created) is the cheapest fix for dropouts. The minimum is 5 seconds. Changing anything here reloads the integration.

data_description.realtime: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.fast: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.medium: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.
data_description.slowest: Seconds between reads, or 0 for never.

permissions.name: Permissions
permissions.description: Who may call the start and stop actions, and who may press the control write test's button. Administrators only is the default: a stopped inverter stays stopped until somebody starts it. Users means users who can already change this device; read-only logins never can, and automations and scripts are not affected. Every other setting is an entity, and Home Assistant decides who may change it: make an account read-only under Settings → People to keep a person from changing any of them.

data_description.start_stop: Who may call the start and stop actions on this inverter.
data_description.capability_test: Administrators only by default. The control write test changes settings on the inverter and puts them back, and — where you have allowed it above — stops and restarts it. Opening it to users means users who can already change this device; a read-only login still cannot.

external.name: Another inverter on the same supply
external.description: This inverter works out your house load from its own production and its grid meter, so a second, non-Sungrow inverter makes the load read low by exactly what it makes. {reported_load} Pick the entities that report the other inverter's power, and two corrected sensors are added. For energy in kWh, add it as a solar source on the Energy dashboard instead. A source that reports unavailable overnight makes the corrected sensors unknown overnight too, rather than assuming zero.

data.external_sources: Power sensors for the other generation

data_description.external_sources: Only power sensors are listed. Pick every one that reports generation this Sungrow cannot see; leave empty to switch the correction off.
data_description.external_placement: This changes the arithmetic, so it is asked rather than guessed.

advanced.name: Battery, wallbox and diagnostics
advanced.description: Battery charge power: {battery_status} Leave it at 0 to let the integration work it out. Otherwise take your datasheet's recommended charge current times the low end of the voltage range, not the nominal voltage (25 A at 355 V is about 8875 W), and round down. Download diagnostics on the device page describes this setup, with the serial number and address removed.

data.register_dump: Include a raw register dump in diagnostics
data.wallbox_host: Wallbox address, when it is on the network itself

data_description.battery_max_power: 0 means work it out: a Sungrow pack is identified from the capacity it reports and looked up against its datasheet, and any other pack that reports a BMS charge current gets that instead. Set a value to override either.
data_description.register_dump: Adds every mapped register's raw value. Only useful when a value looks wrong and the decoding itself is in question. Producing it is a second full read of the register map on top of normal polling, which is slow over a WiNet-S dongle, so leave it off unless you have been asked for it.
data_description.wallbox_host: Only for a Sungrow wallbox with a network cable or WiFi of its own. Without this, the integration finds a wallbox behind a WiNet-S by itself, and that is all most installations need. With it, the wallbox is read at its own address instead -- encrypted, on port 516 -- which also works when this entry is on the inverter's own LAN port, where a wallbox cannot otherwise be seen. Its entities and their history stay as they are. Leave empty to go back to the WiNet-S.

diagnosis.name: Contribute a capability diagnosis
diagnosis.description: Which registers an inverter answers is measured, not looked up, and a reading from yours is what improves support for it. {measured} Everything below is optional and answers what no register can; an empty field records that the question was not answered. capability_test.name: What the control write test may do
capability_test.description: Run diagnosis with capability tests on the device page writes each setting, reads it straight back against Sungrow's specification and puts your value back: the only way to catch a value written at ten times what you asked. Anything that could not be put back becomes a repair that restores it. The six switches below go further, and each is on until you switch it off: pressing the button is your consent. What you switch off stays off.

data.capability_test_restart: May it stop and restart the inverter?
data.capability_test_export_limit: May it switch feed-in limitation on?
data.capability_test_pv_cut: May it cut PV generation for about a minute?
data.capability_test_charge_window: May it set a forced-charging window around now?
data.capability_test_discharge_window: May it move the discharge windows away from now?
data.capability_test_import_limit: May it cap grid import during a short forced charge?

data_description.capability_test_restart:
On unless you switch it off. With this on, the test writes the stop register, waits for the inverter to report itself stopped, starts it again and times all three transitions, so each model's figures are on record.

While it is stopped you generate nothing, the battery neither charges nor discharges, and anything on a backup circuit loses power. Measured so far: stopped within about 2 seconds, running again after 3 to 4 minutes in daylight and over 6 at night, generating up to 20 seconds later. The inverter is never left stopped: the start is retried on fresh connections, it is started again if Home Assistant shuts down mid-test, and if all of that fails you get a repair that starts it.
data_description.capability_test_export_limit:
On unless you switch it off. Where you already limit feed-in, the test uses that and this changes nothing. With this on it may also switch the limit on for about a minute where you do not.

It is the one setting whose failed restore costs you something ongoing rather than just accuracy: an export limit that did not get switched back means you feed in less than you could. If that happens you get a repair here that switches it back.
data_description.capability_test_pv_cut:
On unless you switch it off. With this on, and where your inverter answers register 31211, the test writes the code that stops PV generation, checks that DC power falls to zero, and allows PV again. Generation stops for about half a minute and takes up to a minute more to come back while the inverter searches for its operating point again; the battery and the grid cover the house meanwhile.

This register is not in Sungrow's documentation, which is why the **Cut PV generation** switch is offered only on firmware where this check has passed. A run on yours is how your firmware gets on that list.
data_description.capability_test_charge_window: On unless you switch it off. With this on, and where your inverter has the forced-charging schedule and it is off, the test writes a window around the inverter's own clock with a target a few percent above the battery, switches the schedule on, checks that the battery starts charging, and switches it off again. The battery charges for a minute or two, from the grid if there is no sun. Every word of the schedule is put back afterwards. Skipped where your own schedule is on.
data_description.capability_test_discharge_window:
On unless you switch it off. With this on, and where your inverter answers the discharge schedules (registers 33151-33187), the test moves every weekday and weekend discharge window away from now, checks that the battery stops discharging, and puts every window back. For a minute or two the house imports instead of using the battery.

These registers are not in Sungrow's documentation, which is why they are offered only as readings. A run on yours is the evidence that writing them does what it should.
data_description.capability_test_import_limit:
On unless you switch it off. With this on, and where your inverter answers register 32998, the grid import limit, the test force-charges the battery, sets the limit halfway between what the house then imports and what it would import without the charge, checks that grid import comes down to it, and puts your limit back. It then writes three limits at the ends of the range once each, to record which ones the inverter refuses. The battery charges for about two minutes, from the grid if there is no sun.

This register is not in Sungrow's documentation, which is why it is offered only as a reading. A run on yours is the evidence that writing it does what it should.

promote.title: Set up the devices
promote.description:
Home Assistant found **{count} entities** from the `modbus_sungrow.yaml` package, such as `{example}`. Your recorder history, your statistics and every dashboard card are stored against those entity IDs.

{status}

**Migrate my existing entities** takes those IDs over. History and statistics carry on uninterrupted and your dashboards keep working unchanged. Nothing is copied and nothing is deleted.

**Start fresh** gives this inverter its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_pv_input_power`. Your old history stays where it is, under the old IDs, and your dashboards keep pointing at it.

Either way the entities are identical in every other respect.

data_description.entity_ids: This can be changed later without losing anything.

slot_unknown.title: Set up the devices
slot_unknown.description:
This house ran the YAML package for more than one inverter, and Home Assistant cannot tell which of them this one was. The package's serial sensors are what say so, and neither the running package nor the recorded history has this inverter's serial.

So the YAML package's entity IDs are not offered: taking the wrong set would give this inverter another inverter's history. **Submit** sets it up with its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_pv_input_power`.

To keep its old IDs, put the YAML package back for one restart, so this inverter's serial is recorded, then remove it and restart again. **Configure** can then switch this inverter to its old IDs; the serial stays on record for the recorder's retention, ten days unless you changed it.

other_inverter.title: What is the other inverter?
other_inverter.description:
The make, and its size if you know it — *Fronius Symo 8.2*, or *5 kW string inverter on the south roof*. The size is the useful part: it says how large the gap in the load figures is.

This goes into the document, so leave out serial numbers, addresses and names. You can leave it blank.

entity_ids_legacy.title: Move to the YAML package's entity IDs

entity_ids_modern.title: Move to device-scoped entity IDs
entity_ids_modern.description:
The entities take IDs named after this device, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_pv_input_power`. Their history and statistics move with them.

{changes}{status}

Nothing is copied and nothing is deleted. Names, areas and other settings you gave the entities stay with them. Dashboards, automations and scripts that use the old IDs are not rewritten, so check them afterwards.

You can move back here at any time.

error.nothing_left_to_poll: Every group is set to never, which would leave the integration with nothing to read and no entities at all. Leave at least one group with an interval.
error.wallbox_not_found: No Sungrow wallbox answered at that address. It has to be the wallbox's own address (not the inverter's or the WiNet-S's), reachable from Home Assistant, and not busy with another client.
error.legacy_package_still_loaded: The YAML package is still running, so its entities still hold their IDs. Remove `modbus_sungrow.yaml` from your configuration, restart Home Assistant and try again.
error.legacy_slot_unknown: This house ran the YAML package for more than one inverter, and Home Assistant cannot tell which of them this one was, so the old IDs could be another inverter's. Put the YAML package back for one restart, so this inverter's serial is recorded, then remove it, restart again and come back here.

progress.running_diagnosis: Reading your inverter: 19 capability probes. Through a WiNet-S this can take a minute.

abort.devices_mode_not_offered: Setting up sensors and controls is not in this release. This alpha creates diagnostics-only entries; start again and choose **Perform the device diagnosis**.

run_capability_test.name: Run diagnosis with capability tests
run_capability_test.description: Writes to every control this integration can write to, checks each one three ways and puts it back. Unlike the capability diagnosis, this CHANGES SETTINGS on the inverter: it limits the battery and the export, and it briefly forces a charge and a discharge. Everything is recorded before the first write and restored afterwards, and the run reports anything it could not put back. It exists because a wrong scale is invisible to a readback -- write 700 W, get 700 W back -- and only writing can find it. The restart and export-limit permissions are set in the integration's options and are off by default.

device_id.name: Device
device_id.description: The Sungrow device to write to, and put back.

forced_startup.name: Forced startup only
forced_startup.description: Instead of the capability test, test forced startup under low SoC: with the inverter in standby because its battery is at the minimum and there is no PV, write 0xAA to register 13017, watch the inverter start, write 0x55, watch it go back to standby, and restore the register. Refused in any other state.

run_diagnosis.name: Run read-only diagnosis
run_diagnosis.description: Reads this installation's registers and produces a document describing what answered, so support for it can be measured rather than guessed. Reads only; nothing is written to the inverter, and the serial number is replaced by a stand-in. The finished document arrives as a notification with a download link.

start_inverter.name: Start inverter
start_inverter.description: Boots an inverter that has been shut down. Deliberately an action rather than a button: Home Assistant has no confirmation dialog for a button press, and admin rights are required to call this.

stop_inverter.name: Stop inverter
stop_inverter.description: Shuts the inverter down. It stops generating, stops charging and stops discharging until it is started again. Deliberately an action rather than a button, and admin rights are required to call it — a dashboard card cannot do this by accident.

device_not_found.message: No device with ID {device_id} exists. If this call came from a script, the device may have been removed and re-added since it was written.

entry_not_loaded.message: {title} is not loaded, so it cannot be started or stopped. Check the integration page for a setup error.

not_a_sungrow_device.message: {name} is not a Sungrow Modbus device.

diagnosis_already_running.message: A diagnosis is already running on this inverter. Two at once would compete for one of its very few Modbus connections.

not_on_string_inverter.message: {title} is a string inverter. This action writes to a hybrid inverter's registers, and nothing in this integration writes to a string inverter.

write_scale_unread.message: Could not write {entity_id}: could not read the export limit's bounds to work out this inverter's write scale: {error}

setup_unreachable.message: Could not reach {title}: {error}. A Sungrow inverter accepts very few Modbus connections at once, so check whether something else is polling it -- the modbus_sungrow.yaml package, another Home Assistant, or another tool.

identity_unread.message: Could not read the identity of {title}: {error}

no_serial.message: {title} answered but reported no serial number, so its entities cannot be identified. Please open an issue with the model and firmware version.

firmware_unread.message: Could not read the firmware of {title}: {error}

nothing_to_poll.message: Every poll tier of {title} is set to never, so there is nothing to read. Set at least one interval in the integration's options.

connection_lost.message: Lost the connection to the inverter: {error}. A Sungrow inverter accepts very few Modbus connections at once, so check whether something else is polling it -- the modbus_sungrow.yaml package, another Home Assistant, or another tool.
